title: Name the pattern, not the person
body: "This is the third time a deadline slipped without a heads-up" lands better than "you're unreliable." One is a fact about the situation; the other is an attack on identity.

title: Thoughtful disagreement
body: The greatest tragedy of mankind comes from the inability of people to have thoughtful disagreement to find out what is true.
author: Ray Dalio

title: The team split in two
body: Two senior engineers have an ongoing technical disagreement that is splitting the team into camps. What is the highest-leverage move?

options.label: Make the call yourself and end the debate
Get both in a room and have each restate the other's position before either can rebut it
Avoid the topic in meetings going forward
Move one of them to another team

explanation: Forcing each side to accurately restate the other's position first reveals whether this is a real disagreement or a misunderstanding — most 'unsolvable' conflicts are the latter.

title: The political conflict that wasn't
body: Two peers escalated a fight about system ownership, each convinced the other was being political. A 20-minute conversation revealed they had separately agreed to different things with a third team weeks earlier. Most 'personality conflicts' are unresolved facts wearing a costume.

title: Book the conversation you're avoiding
body: Identify the conflict you've been putting off this week. Book 30 minutes with that person before Friday.

title: Solve it at the smallest scope possible
body: A two-person disagreement solved in a team meeting embarrasses people and rarely beats what a direct, private conversation would have produced.

title: Ask what they are optimizing for
body: Most conflict is two reasonable people optimizing for different, unstated goals. Make the goals explicit and the disagreement often resolves itself.

title: Ask what would change their mind
body: "What would need to be true for you to see it differently?" turns a positional fight into a search for missing information — and often reveals there was no real disagreement on the facts at all.

title: Address it within 24 hours of noticing it
body: The longer you sit on a visible tension, the more both sides build a private story about the other — and the harder the real conversation gets.

title: The conflict routed through the manager
body: Two leads stopped speaking directly and started routing every disagreement through their shared manager, who became a bottleneck for things that should have taken five minutes. Unresolved conflict does not disappear — it finds the most expensive path available.

title: Separate the what from the how
body: Two people can fully agree on the goal and still fight hard over the approach. Naming the shared goal first lowers the temperature before tackling the real disagreement.

title: Name your own defensiveness out loud
body: Next time you feel defensive mid-conversation, say it out loud: "I notice I'm getting defensive — let me actually hear this." It resets the conversation more than you'd expect.

title: Apologize for the impact, not just the intent
body: "I didn't mean it that way" defends you. "I can see how that landed badly, I'm sorry" repairs the relationship. Only one of those is actually an apology.

title: A disagreement about to go external
body: An internal disagreement is about to spill into a meeting with a client or executive. What's the move?

options.label: Hash it out openly in front of them — transparency is good
Agree beforehand to present a united front, and resolve the disagreement separately afterward
Let whoever is more senior decide on the spot
Avoid the meeting until it is resolved

explanation: A visible internal split in front of outside stakeholders damages trust far more than taking one more day to resolve the disagreement privately would cost.

title: An escalation is usually a request for a decision
body: When someone escalates, they usually want a decision made at a higher level — not sympathy. Treat it as a decision request and the interaction gets much shorter.
